# Overview

## Question and hypothesis

**Central question of the project.** Do schizophrenia (SCZ) and bipolar disorder (BD) share cell-type-specific
molecular alterations in the human prefrontal cortex, and could these changes reflect accelerated ageing and
affect neuronal and glial signalling networks?

**Question of this notebook (Q3).** *Do distinct transcriptional signatures converge on common biological pathways,
particularly synaptic and neurotransmission-related ones?*

**Hypothesis tested (H1).** SCZ and BD may affect **the same biological functions**, even if the genes that change
are not the same.

## Why move from genes to pathways

Q2 tells us **which genes** change in each cell type. But two diseases can change few genes in common and still
disturb the same function: a pathway contains dozens of genes, and each disease may hit a different subset of them.
Q3 groups genes into **gene sets** (lists of genes known to work together, for example "synaptic vesicle cycle") and
asks which functions are altered, in SCZ, in BD, and in both.

| Notebook | Answers | Gives to Q3 |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| Q1 – altered populations | *where?* which cell types are most affected | the key cell types to look at first |
| Q2 – pseudobulk DE | *what?* which genes change in SCZ and in BD | the table of all tested genes and their statistics |
| **Q3 – this notebook** | ***which functions?*** do the changes converge on the same pathways | — |
| Q4 – cell communication | *which signals?* | pathways involving ligands / receptors can be checked in Q4 |

## Two methods, used one after the other: ORA, then GSEA

We follow the usual `clusterProfiler` workflow [1–3]: the official clusterProfiler book [1] and the HBC Training lesson
on pseudobulk data [2], which is exactly our Q2 → Q3 situation.

- **ORA (over-representation analysis)** takes the list of significant genes (DEGs) and asks: *does this list contain
  more genes of a given function than expected by chance?* It is simple and close to the Q2 results, but it depends on
  the significance threshold.
- **GSEA (gene set enrichment analysis)** [4] takes **all** tested genes, ranked from the most increased to the most
  decreased, and asks: *are the genes of a function grouped at the top or at the bottom of this ranking?* It needs no
  threshold and gives a direction (up or down). It can detect a function where many genes change a little, which is
  exactly what H1 predicts if SCZ and BD reach the same function through different genes.

Results found by **both** methods are the most reliable.

| | ORA | GSEA |
|---|---|---|
| Input | list of DEGs (adjusted p < 0.05) | all tested genes, ranked |
| Direction of the change | only if up and down genes are tested separately | yes, given by the sign of the NES |
| Detects | functions with several strongly changed genes | functions with many slightly changed genes |
| `clusterProfiler` functions | `enrichGO()`, `enricher()`, `compareCluster()` | `gseGO()`, `GSEA()` |

# Setup

| Package | Used for |
|---------|----------|
| `clusterProfiler` | ORA and GSEA (topic of a CC2 video) |
| `org.Hs.eg.db` | human gene annotation: links gene symbols to GO terms |
| `enrichplot` | standard enrichment figures: `dotplot`, `cnetplot`, `gseaplot2` |
| `dplyr`, `tidyr`, `ggplot2`, `ggrepel` | tables and figures |

```{r setup}
the.seed <- 42          # GSEA uses random permutations: a fixed seed makes the results reproducible
set.seed(the.seed)

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr)
  library(tidyr)
  library(ggplot2)
  library(ggrepel)
  library(clusterProfiler)
  library(enrichplot)
  library(org.Hs.eg.db)
})

# Reusable functions, kept outside the notebook so the code below stays readable
source("R/utils_genesets.R")
source("R/utils_enrichment.R")
source("R/utils_figures.R")     # common figure style, colours and saving (shared with the other notebooks)
```

All the choices are gathered in one place, so the analysis can be re-run with other values.

| Parameter | Value | Why |
|-----------|-------|-----|
| `alpha` | 0.05 | threshold on the **adjusted** p-value (Benjamini–Hochberg correction, because thousands of tests are done) |
| `min_set_size` / `max_set_size` | 15 / 500 | very small sets give unstable results; very large ones are too vague to interpret |
| `ranking_metric` | `stat` | DESeq2 Wald statistic = log2 fold change divided by its uncertainty. It ranks genes by how **confidently** they change, keeps the direction, and avoids favouring noisy, lowly expressed genes |
| `simplify_cutoff` | 0.7 | GO terms that are too similar are merged, keeping the most significant one |
| `key_celltypes` | from Q1 | cell types shown in the detailed figures (all cell types are analysed and saved) |
| `overview_collection` | Hallmark | collection used in the overview figures: 50 well-known processes with readable names |

```{r parameters}
# Inputs
de_path    <- "../03_RESULTS/Q2_pseudobulk_DE/de_results_all.csv"
geneset_dir <- "../01_DATA/genesets"   # one CSV per collection (gs_name, gene_symbol), see its README.md

# Outputs
out_dir <- "../03_RESULTS/Q3_enrichment"
fig_dir <- "../04_FIGURES/Q3"
dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create(fig_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

# Analysis choices
alpha               <- 0.05
min_set_size        <- 15
max_set_size        <- 500
ranking_metric      <- "stat"
simplify_cutoff     <- 0.7
contrast_scz        <- "SCZ_vs_CTRL"
contrast_bd         <- "BD_vs_CTRL"
contrast_direct     <- "SCZ_vs_BD"   # direct comparison of the two disorders (provided by Q2)
q1_path             <- "../03_RESULTS/Q1_composition/Q1_populations_retenues.txt"   # cell types retained in Q1
key_celltypes       <- if (file.exists(q1_path)) readLines(q1_path) else
                         c("Micro", "Oligo", "EN_L5_6_NP", "EN_L6_IT_1", "EN_L6_IT_2", "EN_L6B", "EN_L6_CT")
key_celltypes       <- key_celltypes[nzchar(key_celltypes)]
overview_collection <- "Hallmark"

# Short labels for the three comparisons, and their full names for the legends
label_contrast <- function(x) {
  factor(dplyr::recode(x, !!contrast_scz := "SCZ", !!contrast_bd := "BD", !!contrast_direct := "SCZ vs BD"),
         levels = c("SCZ", "BD", "SCZ vs BD"))
}
lab_disease <- c(SCZ = "SCZ vs controls", BD = "BD vs controls", "SCZ vs BD" = "SCZ vs BD (direct)")

# NES colour scale: purple = shifted down, orange = shifted up
# (not blue / red, which already mean SCZ / BD in every figure)
scale_fill_nes <- function(lim) {
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#5e3c99", mid = "white", high = "#e66101", midpoint = 0,
                       limits = c(-lim, lim), name = "NES")
}
# Adjusted p-value scale of the enrichplot dot plots: dark purple = most significant
scale_padj <- list(
  scale_colour_gradient(low = "#5b1f75", high = "#e2a9f1", name = "Adjusted p-value"),
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#5b1f75", high = "#e2a9f1", name = "Adjusted p-value")
)
scale_colour_nes <- function(lim) {
  scale_colour_gradient2(low = "#5e3c99", mid = "grey90", high = "#e66101", midpoint = 0,
                         limits = c(-lim, lim), name = "NES")
}
```

# Step 1 – The input: Q2 results

**What we do and why.** Before any enrichment, we check that the Q2 table is complete and see how many genes change
in each cell type. The table has one row per gene, cell type and comparison, with the DESeq2 results:
`log2FoldChange` (size and direction of the change), `stat` (used to rank genes), and `padj` (p-value adjusted for the
number of genes tested). **All tested genes** are kept, not only the significant ones: the GSEA needs the full ranking,
and the ORA needs them as the background ("universe").

```{r load-de}
de <- load_de_results(de_path)   # stops with a clear message if a column is missing

cell_types    <- sort(unique(de$cell_type))
key_celltypes <- intersect(key_celltypes, cell_types)

deg_counts <- de |>
  mutate(disease = label_contrast(contrast)) |>
  group_by(cell_type, disease) |>
  summarise(n_tested = n(),
            up       = sum(padj < alpha & log2FoldChange > 0, na.rm = TRUE),
            down     = sum(padj < alpha & log2FoldChange < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups  = "drop")
deg_counts
```

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
One row per cell type and comparison. `n_tested` = number of genes analysed (expressed enough in that cell type to be
tested); `up` / `down` = number of genes significantly increased / decreased (adjusted p < `r alpha`). For
`SCZ vs BD`, "up" means higher in SCZ than in BD. The DEGs themselves are described in Q2; here we only check that
there is enough signal for the enrichment.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Interpretation [to fill]"}
- Which cell types have the most DEGs in SCZ? In BD? Is it consistent with Q1?
- When a list has fewer than 5 genes, ORA cannot be run on it; GSEA (Part B) can still find pathway changes there.
- Few donors or few nuclei mean less power: note it as a limit.
:::

**Quick check of the gene ranking.** The GSEA ranks genes by the Wald statistic. If Q2 worked well, most genes do not
change, so the statistic should be centred on 0 (median close to 0). A median far from 0 would point to a problem in Q2
(for example a missing covariate).

```{r ranking-check}
de |>
  mutate(disease = label_contrast(contrast)) |>
  group_by(cell_type, disease) |>
  summarise(median_stat = round(median(.data[[ranking_metric]], na.rm = TRUE), 2),
            q05 = round(quantile(.data[[ranking_metric]], 0.05, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
            q95 = round(quantile(.data[[ranking_metric]], 0.95, na.rm = TRUE), 2),
            .groups = "drop")
```

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
`median_stat` should be close to 0. `q05` and `q95` give the range of 90 % of the genes: a wider range means a stronger
response to the disease.
:::

# Step 2 – Gene sets: which functions are tested?

**What we do and why.** We use four collections of gene sets, from broad to specialised. P-values are corrected
**within each collection**, because the collections overlap and answer different questions.

| Collection | Size | Why |
|------------|------|-----|
| GO Biological Process | ~7,500 terms | detailed functions; similar terms are merged with `simplify()` |
| MSigDB Hallmark [5] | 50 sets | well-known processes (inflammation, oxidative phosphorylation...): a readable overview |
| Reactome | ~1,600 pathways | signalling and metabolic pathways, including neurotransmission |
| SynGO [6] | expert-curated synaptic genes | direct test of the synaptic part of the question (file in `01_DATA/genesets/`, see its `README.md`) |

GO is read with `org.Hs.eg.db`; Hallmark, Reactome (MSigDB v7.5.1) and SynGO are CSV files included in
`01_DATA/genesets/`, so no download is needed. Gene symbols are used everywhere, so no
identifier conversion is needed.

```{r gene-sets}
# NULL = GO Biological Process, handled by enrichGO / gseGO with org.Hs.eg.db
collections <- list(GO_BP    = NULL,
                    Hallmark = read_geneset_file(file.path(geneset_dir, "Q3_hallmark.csv")),
                    Reactome = read_geneset_file(file.path(geneset_dir, "Q3_reactome.csv")),
                    SynGO    = read_geneset_file(file.path(geneset_dir, "Q3_syngo.csv")))
if (is.null(collections$SynGO)) {
  collections$SynGO <- NULL   # removes the empty entry
  cat("Note: SynGO file not found, Step 9 will be skipped.\n")
}

msigdb_like <- collections[!vapply(collections, is.null, logical(1))]

# How many genes of each set were actually tested in Q2?
tested_genes <- unique(de$gene)
bind_rows(lapply(names(msigdb_like), function(coll) {
  cbind(collection = coll, geneset_coverage(term2gene_to_list(msigdb_like[[coll]]), tested_genes))
})) |>
  group_by(collection) |>
  summarise(n_sets                    = n(),
            median_fraction_present   = round(median(fraction_present), 2),
            sets_with_less_than_50pct = sum(fraction_present < 0.5),
            .groups = "drop")
```

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
A gene set is only reliable if most of its genes were tested in Q2. `median_fraction_present` is the typical fraction
of a set's genes found in our data. Sets with less than 50 % of their genes present are mostly made of genes not
expressed in the cortex (for example liver or immune genes). GO is not shown: `clusterProfiler` handles it
automatically.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Interpretation [to fill]"}
- Is the coverage good for synaptic sets? It should be, in brain tissue.
- If a collection has poor coverage, interpret it with more caution.
:::

# Part A – Over-representation analysis (ORA)

**How ORA works.** Take the DEGs of one cell type and one gene set. If the set contains 2 % of all tested genes but
10 % of the DEGs, it is over-represented. A hypergeometric test (a one-sided Fisher test) says whether this excess is
larger than chance. `clusterProfiler` reports it as `GeneRatio` (DEGs in the set / all DEGs) against `BgRatio` (tested
genes in the set / all tested genes).

**Our choices.**

- Up- and down-regulated genes are tested **separately**: otherwise we could not tell whether a function goes up or down.
- The background (**universe**) is the set of genes tested in Q2 for that cell type, not the whole genome. With the
  whole genome, every brain function would look enriched, only because genes not expressed in the brain can never be DEGs.
- `compareCluster()` runs the ORA on the four lists of a cell type (SCZ up, SCZ down, BD up, BD down) together, so SCZ
  and BD can be compared on the same figure.
- Lists with fewer than 5 genes are skipped.

# Step 3 – Which functions are over-represented among the DEGs?

## GO Biological Process

```{r ora-go, cache=TRUE, cache.extra=tools::md5sum(de_path)}
ora_go <- list()
for (ct in cell_types) {
  de_ct    <- de[de$cell_type == ct, ]
  lists    <- make_deg_lists(de_ct, alpha, c(SCZ = contrast_scz, BD = contrast_bd))
  universe <- unique(de_ct$gene)
  res <- run_ora_compare(lists, universe, term2gene = NULL, alpha = alpha,
                         min_size = min_set_size, max_size = max_set_size)
  if (!is.null(res)) ora_go[[ct]] <- simplify_go(res, cutoff = simplify_cutoff)
}

ora_go_table <- bind_rows(lapply(names(ora_go), function(ct) {
  cbind(cell_type = ct, as.data.frame(ora_go[[ct]]))
}))
if (nrow(ora_go_table) > 0) {
  write.csv(ora_go_table, file.path(out_dir, "ora_go_bp.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
  count(ora_go_table, cell_type, Cluster) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = Cluster, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
}
```

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
Number of significant GO terms per cell type and gene list, after merging similar terms. A missing column means that
the list had fewer than 5 genes or no significant term.
:::

**Why merge GO terms.** GO is organised as a tree: "chemical synaptic transmission" is inside "synaptic signalling",
so the same genes give many almost identical terms. `simplify()` merges terms whose similarity is above
`r simplify_cutoff` and keeps the most significant one.

```{r fig-F01, fig.width=10, fig.height=7}
for (ct in intersect(key_celltypes, names(ora_go))) {
  p <- dotplot(clean_result_names(ora_go[[ct]]), showCategory = 5, label_format = 45) +
    labs(x = "Gene list (number of DEGs in brackets)",
         y = "GO Biological Process term",
         size = "Gene ratio", colour = "Adjusted p-value", fill = "Adjusted p-value",
         title = paste0(ct, ": GO terms over-represented among the DEGs"),
         subtitle = "ORA on GO Biological Process (similar terms merged), 5 most significant terms per gene list",
         caption = "Gene ratio = fraction of the list's DEGs that belong to the term.") +
    scale_padj +
    theme_project() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1), legend.position = "right")
  print(p)
  save_figure(p, paste0("Q3_F01_ORA_GO_", ct), fig_dir, width = 10, height = 7)
}
```

**Figure Q3-F01 – GO Biological Process terms over-represented among the DEGs (one figure per key cell type).**
Over-representation analysis (`compareCluster`, `enrichGO`) of up- and down-regulated DEGs (adjusted p < 0.05) in SCZ
and BD, against all genes tested in the same cell type. Redundant terms were merged (`simplify`, cutoff 0.7). Dot size:
gene ratio; colour: adjusted p-value (Benjamini–Hochberg).

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
Columns = the four gene lists of the cell type; rows = GO terms. A dot means the term is over-represented in that list.
Bigger dot = larger part of the list in the term; redder dot = more significant. A row with dots in both `SCZ_down`
and `BD_down` (or both `_up` columns) is a function changed in the same way by both diseases.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Interpretation [to fill]"}
- Are the **same terms** found in SCZ and BD lists of the same direction? This is a first sign of convergence.
- In neurons, are synaptic terms found among down-regulated genes? In glia, inflammatory or immune terms among
  up-regulated genes?
- Note 2–3 terms per cell type to discuss in the report, with a few of their genes (column `geneID` of
  `ora_go_bp.csv`).
:::

## Hallmark, Reactome and SynGO

The same ORA is run on the other collections, with `enricher()`.

```{r ora-curated, cache=TRUE, cache.extra=tools::md5sum(de_path)}
ora_curated_table <- bind_rows(lapply(names(msigdb_like), function(coll) {
  bind_rows(lapply(cell_types, function(ct) {
    de_ct <- de[de$cell_type == ct, ]
    res <- run_ora_compare(make_deg_lists(de_ct, alpha, c(SCZ = contrast_scz, BD = contrast_bd)),
                           unique(de_ct$gene), term2gene = msigdb_like[[coll]], alpha = alpha,
                           min_size = min_set_size, max_size = max_set_size)
    if (is.null(res)) return(NULL)
    cbind(collection = coll, cell_type = ct, as.data.frame(res))
  }))
}))

if (nrow(ora_curated_table) > 0) {
  write.csv(ora_curated_table, file.path(out_dir, "ora_curated.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
}
```

```{r ora-curated-table}
# 3 most significant sets per collection, cell type and list
ora_curated_table |>
  group_by(collection, cell_type, Cluster) |>
  slice_min(p.adjust, n = 3, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  mutate(set = clean_set_name(Description)) |>
  select(collection, cell_type, Cluster, set, GeneRatio, BgRatio, p.adjust)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
For each collection, cell type and gene list, the 3 most significant sets. `GeneRatio` = DEGs in the set / DEGs in the
list; `BgRatio` = tested genes in the set / all tested genes. A set is enriched when `GeneRatio` is clearly larger than
`BgRatio`.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Interpretation [to fill]"}
- Do the Hallmark and Reactome results tell the same story as GO?
- Any SynGO term in the neuronal down-regulated lists?
:::

# Step 4 – Do SCZ and BD change the same genes?

**What we do and why.** Before comparing functions, we measure how much the two diseases share at the **gene** level.
Each gene of a cell type is classified as a DEG in both diseases in the same direction (shared), in one disease only,
or in both with opposite directions. The overlap is summarised by the **Jaccard index**: shared DEGs / all DEGs
(0 = no gene in common, 1 = identical lists). H1 predicts a low overlap of genes, but a larger overlap of functions
(Steps 6–7). Q2 already describes shared and specific DEGs; here we only compute the value that Figure F06 compares
with the pathway level.

```{r deg-overlap}
deg_status <- de |>
  filter(contrast %in% c(contrast_scz, contrast_bd)) |>
  mutate(direction = case_when(padj < alpha & log2FoldChange > 0 ~ "up",
                               padj < alpha & log2FoldChange < 0 ~ "down",
                               TRUE ~ "ns"),
         contrast = recode(contrast, !!contrast_scz := "SCZ", !!contrast_bd := "BD")) |>
  select(cell_type, gene, contrast, direction) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = contrast, values_from = direction, values_fill = "ns") |>
  mutate(group = case_when(SCZ != "ns" & SCZ == BD ~ "shared",
                           SCZ != "ns" & BD == "ns" ~ "SCZ_only",
                           SCZ == "ns" & BD != "ns" ~ "BD_only",
                           SCZ != "ns" & BD != "ns" ~ "opposite",
                           TRUE ~ "ns"))

deg_overlap <- deg_status |>
  filter(group != "ns") |>
  count(cell_type, group) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
for (g in c("shared", "SCZ_only", "BD_only", "opposite")) if (!g %in% names(deg_overlap)) deg_overlap[[g]] <- 0
deg_overlap <- deg_overlap |>
  mutate(n_DEG = shared + SCZ_only + BD_only + opposite,
         jaccard_DEG = round(shared / n_DEG, 2))
deg_overlap
```

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
Number of genes per cell type that are DEGs in both diseases with the same direction (`shared`), in one disease only
(`SCZ_only`, `BD_only`), or in both with opposite directions (`opposite`). `jaccard_DEG` = shared / all DEGs.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Interpretation [to fill]"}
- Is the gene-level overlap low (J close to 0)? In which cell types is it highest? Keep these values: they are shown
  again in Figure F06.
:::

# Part B – Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA)

**How GSEA works.** All tested genes are ranked from the most up-regulated to the most down-regulated (Wald statistic).
For each gene set, the method walks down the ranking: a running score goes up each time it meets a gene of the set and
goes down otherwise. If the genes of the set are grouped at the top, the score reaches a high positive peak (the set is
shifted **up** in the disease); at the bottom, a negative peak (shifted **down**). This peak is normalised for the size
of the set, giving the **NES** (normalised enrichment score): its sign gives the direction, its size the strength.
Random permutations give the p-value. The genes before the peak, which drive the result, form the **leading edge**.

**Our choices.**

- `gseGO()` for GO, `GSEA()` for Hallmark, Reactome and SynGO.
- All tested sets are kept (`pvalueCutoff = 1`), so SCZ and BD can be compared on exactly the same sets; the 0.05
  threshold is applied afterwards.
- `eps = 0` to compute very small p-values exactly; fixed seed for reproducibility.
- The same GSEA is run on the direct `SCZ_vs_BD` comparison, used in Step 6.

# Step 5 – Which pathways are shifted, in which cell types?

```{r gsea, cache=TRUE, cache.extra=tools::md5sum(de_path)}
gsea_all <- lapply(names(collections), function(coll) {
  res <- run_gsea_all(de, collections[[coll]],
                      metric   = ranking_metric,
                      min_size = min_set_size,
                      max_size = max_set_size,
                      seed     = the.seed)
  if (!is.null(res)) res$collection <- coll
  res
}) |>
  bind_rows() |>
  mutate(disease = label_contrast(contrast))

write.csv(gsea_all, file.path(out_dir, "gsea_all.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

gsea_counts <- gsea_all |>
  group_by(collection, cell_type, disease) |>
  summarise(up   = sum(p.adjust < alpha & NES > 0),
            down = sum(p.adjust < alpha & NES < 0),
            .groups = "drop")
gsea_counts
```

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
Number of significant gene sets (adjusted p < `r alpha`) per collection, cell type and comparison: `up` = sets whose
genes are grouped among up-regulated genes (NES > 0), `down` = among down-regulated genes (NES < 0).
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Interpretation [to fill]"}
- Which cell types show the most pathway changes? Is it the same ranking as for the DEGs (Step 1)? A cell type with
  few DEGs but many shifted pathways shows many small, coordinated changes, which only GSEA can detect.
:::

## Reading one GSEA result in detail

**What we do and why.** Before looking at summaries, we look at one result in detail to see what an NES and a leading
edge are. We take the most significant Hallmark set.

```{r fig-F02, fig.width=9, fig.height=7}
top_hit <- gsea_all |>
  filter(collection == overview_collection, disease %in% c("SCZ", "BD")) |>
  slice_min(p.adjust, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

top_hit |> select(cell_type, disease, ID, setSize, NES, p.adjust)

example_ranks <- make_ranked_list(de[de$cell_type == top_hit$cell_type &
                                     de$contrast == top_hit$contrast, ], ranking_metric)
example_gsea <- run_gsea_object(example_ranks, collections[[overview_collection]],
                                min_set_size, max_set_size, the.seed)
p_F02 <- gseaplot2(example_gsea, geneSetID = top_hit$ID, color = "#8e3fb0")
# gseaplot2 returns 3 stacked panels: add the titles and readable axis names
p_F02[[1]] <- p_F02[[1]] +
  labs(y = "Running enrichment score",
       title = paste0(clean_set_name(top_hit$ID), " in ", top_hit$cell_type, ", ", top_hit$disease, " vs controls"),
       subtitle = paste0("GSEA enrichment plot: NES = ", round(top_hit$NES, 2),
                         ", adjusted p = ", signif(top_hit$p.adjust, 2))) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "#3849a2", size = 13),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey25"))
p_F02[[3]] <- p_F02[[3]] +
  labs(x = "Rank of the gene (left: most up-regulated, right: most down-regulated)",
       y = "Ranking statistic\n(Wald)")
p_F02
save_figure(p_F02, "Q3_F02_GSEA_example", fig_dir, width = 9, height = 7)
```

**Figure Q3-F02 – Example of a GSEA result.** Enrichment plot (`gseaplot2`) of the most significant Hallmark set.
Top: running enrichment score along the ranked gene list (its peak is the enrichment score). Middle: position of each
gene of the set in the ranking. Bottom: ranking statistic (DESeq2 Wald statistic), from up-regulated (left) to
down-regulated (right) genes.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
- A peak on the **left** (positive score): the set's genes are grouped among the up-regulated genes. A dip on the
  **right**: among the down-regulated genes.
- The vertical bars show where the set's genes are: concentrated at one end = strong enrichment.
- The genes between the start of the list and the peak form the **leading edge**.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Interpretation [to fill]"}
- Which set, cell type and disease is the strongest result? Is it expected from the literature?
- Is it carried by many genes (wide peak) or by a few strongly changed genes (sharp peak)?
:::

# Step 6 – SCZ vs BD: shared or specific pathways?

**What we do and why.** For each cell type and gene set, we put the SCZ and BD results side by side and classify the
set. A pathway significant in SCZ but not in BD is not necessarily specific to SCZ: BD may show the same change, but
with fewer donors it does not reach the threshold. To say that the two disorders **differ**, they must be compared
**directly**: Q2 provides this comparison (`SCZ_vs_BD`, patients compared with each other, with the same covariates),
and we ran the same GSEA on it. A disease-specific pathway is therefore called **confirmed** only if the direct test is
also significant.

| Category | Rule | Meaning |
|----------|------|---------|
| Shared, same direction | significant in both diseases vs controls, same sign of NES | common alteration |
| Shared, opposite directions | significant in both, opposite signs | same function, opposite effects |
| SCZ only (or BD only), confirmed | significant in one disease only **and** in the direct SCZ vs BD test | the two disorders differ |
| SCZ only (or BD only), not confirmed | significant in one disease only, direct test not significant | seen in one disease, but no evidence of a difference |
| Not significant | significant in neither | no evidence |

```{r compare}
paired <- gsea_all |>
  group_by(collection) |>
  group_modify(~ pair_contrasts(.x, contrast_scz, contrast_bd)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  classify_pathways(alpha = alpha)

# Add the direct SCZ vs BD test, if this comparison is in the Q2 table
direct <- gsea_all |>
  filter(contrast == contrast_direct) |>
  select(collection, cell_type, ID, NES_direct = NES, p.adjust_direct = p.adjust)
has_direct <- nrow(direct) > 0
if (has_direct) {
  paired <- paired |>
    left_join(direct, by = c("collection", "cell_type", "ID")) |>
    mutate(differs_SCZ_BD = !is.na(p.adjust_direct) & p.adjust_direct < alpha)
} else {
  paired$differs_SCZ_BD <- NA
  cat("Note: no SCZ_vs_BD comparison in the Q2 table, specific pathways cannot be confirmed.\n")
}

# Final category, with the confirmation by the direct test
paired <- paired |>
  mutate(group = case_when(
    category == "shared_concordant" ~ "Shared, same direction",
    category == "shared_opposite"   ~ "Shared, opposite directions",
    category == "SCZ_specific" & !has_direct ~ "SCZ only",
    category == "BD_specific"  & !has_direct ~ "BD only",
    category == "SCZ_specific" & differs_SCZ_BD  ~ "SCZ only, confirmed",
    category == "SCZ_specific" & !differs_SCZ_BD ~ "SCZ only, not confirmed",
    category == "BD_specific"  & differs_SCZ_BD  ~ "BD only, confirmed",
    category == "BD_specific"  & !differs_SCZ_BD ~ "BD only, not confirmed",
    TRUE ~ "Not significant"))

write.csv(paired, file.path(out_dir, "gsea_scz_vs_bd.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

count(paired, collection, group) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
```

```{r fig-F03, fig.width=11, fig.height=6}
col_group <- c("Shared, same direction" = "#8e3fb0", "Shared, opposite directions" = "#f1a340",
               "SCZ only, confirmed" = "#2166ac", "SCZ only, not confirmed" = "#a6c8e6", "SCZ only" = "#2166ac",
               "BD only, confirmed" = "#b2182b", "BD only, not confirmed" = "#f0a8a8", "BD only" = "#b2182b")

p_F03 <- paired |>
  filter(group != "Not significant") |>
  count(collection, cell_type, group) |>
  mutate(group = factor(group, levels = names(col_group))) |>
  ggplot(aes(cell_type, n, fill = group)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.75) +
  facet_wrap(~ collection, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = col_group, name = NULL) +
  guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +
  labs(x = "Cell type", y = "Number of significant gene sets",
       title = "Shared and disease-specific pathways per cell type",
       subtitle = paste0("GSEA, gene sets significant (adjusted p < ", alpha, ") in at least one disease vs controls"),
       caption = "Confirmed = also significant in the direct SCZ vs BD comparison; light colours = seen in one disease only, without evidence of a difference.") +
  theme_project() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
p_F03
save_figure(p_F03, "Q3_F03_pathway_categories", fig_dir, width = 11, height = 6)
```

**Figure Q3-F03 – Shared and disease-specific pathways per cell type.** Number of gene sets significantly shifted
(GSEA, Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted p < 0.05) in at least one disease compared with controls, per collection and cell
type: shared with the same direction (purple), shared with opposite directions (orange), significant in SCZ only (blue)
or BD only (red). Dark blue / dark red: also significant in the direct SCZ vs BD comparison (confirmed difference);
light blue / light red: no significant difference in the direct comparison.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
Each bar counts the altered pathways of a cell type. A large purple part means that many functions are changed in the
same way in both diseases: this is where SCZ and BD converge. Only the **dark** blue and red parts are pathways that
truly differ between the two disorders; the light parts are seen in one disease only, but we cannot say that the two
diseases differ.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Interpretation [to fill]"}
- In which cell types are shared pathways the majority?
- What fraction of the "only" pathways is confirmed? A small fraction means that SCZ and BD are more similar than the
  comparisons with controls suggest (part of the difference is a difference in power).
- Any pathway shared with opposite directions? It would be worth discussing.
:::

**Which pathways differ most between SCZ and BD?**

```{r direct-top}
if (has_direct) {
  paired |>
    filter(differs_SCZ_BD) |>
    arrange(p.adjust_direct) |>
    mutate(set = clean_set_name(Description)) |>
    select(collection, cell_type, set, NES_SCZ, NES_BD, NES_direct, p.adjust_direct, group) |>
    head(15)
}
```

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
The 15 pathways with the most significant direct SCZ vs BD test. `NES_direct` > 0: higher in SCZ than in BD; < 0:
higher in BD. A "shared, same direction" pathway can also appear here: both disorders change it in the same direction,
but with a different strength.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Interpretation [to fill]"}
- Which functions truly differ between SCZ and BD, and in which cell types?
:::

## Do SCZ and BD have similar profiles overall?

**What we do and why.** Beyond significant sets, we compare the NES of **all** tested sets in SCZ and in BD with a
Spearman correlation (rho). A rho close to 1 means that the two diseases shift the same functions in the same direction,
even below the significance threshold.

```{r nes-correlation}
nes_cor <- paired |>
  group_by(collection, cell_type) |>
  summarise(spearman_rho = round(cor(NES_SCZ, NES_BD, method = "spearman"), 2),
            n_sets       = n(),
            .groups = "drop")
nes_cor
```

```{r fig-F04, fig.width=11, fig.height=8}
scatter_data <- paired |>
  filter(collection == overview_collection) |>
  left_join(nes_cor, by = c("collection", "cell_type")) |>
  mutate(panel = paste0(cell_type, " (rho = ", spearman_rho, ")"),
         group = factor(group, levels = c(names(col_group), "Not significant")))
lim_sc <- max(abs(c(scatter_data$NES_SCZ, scatter_data$NES_BD)), na.rm = TRUE)
to_label <- scatter_data |>
  filter(group == "Shared, same direction") |>
  group_by(cell_type) |>
  slice_min(pmax(p.adjust_SCZ, p.adjust_BD), n = 2, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()

p_F04 <- ggplot(scatter_data, aes(NES_SCZ, NES_BD, colour = group)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey75") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey75") +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_text_repel(data = to_label, aes(label = clean_set_name(Description, 30)),
                  size = 2.8, colour = "black", min.segment.length = 0, seed = the.seed) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel) +
  coord_equal(xlim = c(-lim_sc, lim_sc), ylim = c(-lim_sc, lim_sc)) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(col_group, "Not significant" = "grey85"), name = NULL) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2, override.aes = list(size = 3))) +
  labs(x = "NES in SCZ vs controls", y = "NES in BD vs controls",
       title = "NES of the Hallmark processes in SCZ and in BD",
       subtitle = paste0("GSEA on MSigDB ", overview_collection, ": each dot is a gene set; rho = Spearman correlation of the NES"),
       caption = "Dashed line: same NES in both diseases. Labels: the 2 most significant shared sets per cell type.") +
  theme_project()
p_F04
save_figure(p_F04, "Q3_F04_NES_scatter_Hallmark", fig_dir, width = 11, height = 8)
```

**Figure Q3-F04 – Comparison of the pathway profiles of SCZ and BD.** Normalised enrichment score (NES) of each
MSigDB Hallmark set in SCZ vs controls (x) and in BD vs controls (y), per cell type. Colours give the category of Figure
F03. The Spearman correlation (rho) of the NES over all sets is given in each panel title. Dashed line: identity.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
Each dot is a process. Top right: up in both diseases; bottom left: down in both; the two other corners: opposite
directions. Dots close to the dashed diagonal change in the same way in SCZ and BD. A high rho means similar profiles
overall.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Interpretation [to fill]"}
- Do the dots follow the diagonal (high rho)? In which cell types?
- Which processes are the purple (shared) dots? Name the 2–3 most relevant ones for the report.
:::

## The main pathways at a glance

```{r fig-F05, fig.width=12, fig.height=10}
top_sets <- paired |>
  filter(category != "not_significant") |>
  mutate(best_padj = pmin(p.adjust_SCZ, p.adjust_BD)) |>
  group_by(collection, ID) |>
  summarise(best_padj = min(best_padj), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(collection) |>
  slice_min(best_padj, n = 30, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  ungroup()

heat_data <- gsea_all |>
  semi_join(top_sets, by = c("collection", "ID")) |>
  mutate(signif = ifelse(p.adjust < alpha, "*", ""))

# Main collection (Hallmark) for the main text, GO for the appendix; SynGO has its own figure (F07)
for (coll in intersect(c(overview_collection, "GO_BP"), unique(heat_data$collection))) {
  d <- filter(heat_data, collection == coll)
  # order the rows so that sets with similar profiles are next to each other
  wide <- d |>
    filter(disease %in% c("SCZ", "BD")) |>
    mutate(column = paste(disease, cell_type)) |>
    select(ID, column, NES) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = column, values_from = NES, values_fill = 0)
  row_order <- if (nrow(wide) > 2) wide$ID[hclust(dist(as.matrix(wide[, -1])))$order] else wide$ID
  set_labels <- setNames(clean_set_name(d$Description, 55), d$ID)
  lim <- max(abs(d$NES), na.rm = TRUE)

  p <- d |>
    mutate(ID = factor(ID, levels = row_order)) |>
    ggplot(aes(cell_type, ID, fill = NES)) +
    geom_tile(colour = "white") +
    geom_text(aes(label = signif), size = 4, vjust = 0.75) +
    facet_wrap(~ disease, labeller = as_labeller(lab_disease)) +
    scale_fill_nes(lim) +
    scale_y_discrete(labels = set_labels) +
    labs(x = "Cell type", y = NULL,
         title = paste0("Main pathways altered in SCZ and BD (", coll, ")"),
         subtitle = paste0("GSEA NES of the ", length(row_order), " most significant sets; * adjusted p < ", alpha),
         caption = "Orange: set shifted up; purple: shifted down. Right panel: direct comparison (orange = higher in SCZ than in BD).") +
    theme_project() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1), panel.grid = element_blank(),
          legend.position = "right")
  print(p)
  save_figure(p, paste0("Q3_F05_NES_heatmap_", coll), fig_dir, width = 12, height = 2.5 + 0.25 * length(row_order))
}
```

**Figure Q3-F05 – Main pathways altered in SCZ and BD (Hallmark for the main text, GO Biological Process for the appendix).** Normalised enrichment score (NES,
colour) of the 30 most significant gene sets of the collection, per cell type (columns), in SCZ vs controls (left), BD
vs controls (middle) and SCZ vs BD (right). Rows are ordered by hierarchical clustering of the SCZ and BD profiles.
\* adjusted p < 0.05.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
Read the figure row by row: a row with the same colour and a star in the left and middle panels is a function changed
in the same way in both diseases. A star in the right panel means the two diseases differ for that function in that
cell type.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Interpretation [to fill]"}
- Which rows are coloured the same, with stars, in both disease panels? These are the shared functions to highlight.
- Where are the stars of the direct test? Do they match the "confirmed" pathways of Figure F03?
:::

# Step 7 – Same pathway, different genes? (direct test of H1)

**What we do and why.** For a pathway changed in the same direction in both diseases, we look at the genes that drive
it (the leading edge) in SCZ and in BD, and measure their overlap with the Jaccard index:

$$
J = \frac{\text{genes driving the pathway in both diseases}}{\text{genes driving it in at least one disease}}
$$

J = 0: completely different genes; J = 1: the same genes. H1 predicts that shared pathways are reached through partly
different genes, so a J lower than 0.5, and lower than or similar to the gene-level overlap of the DEG lists (Step 4).

```{r leading-edge}
shared <- paired |>
  filter(category == "shared_concordant") |>
  add_leading_edge_overlap()

write.csv(shared, file.path(out_dir, "shared_sets_leading_edge.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

shared |>
  mutate(set = clean_set_name(Description)) |>
  select(collection, cell_type, set, NES_SCZ, NES_BD, leading_edge_jaccard) |>
  arrange(leading_edge_jaccard) |>
  head(15)
```

```{r fig-F06, fig.width=10, fig.height=6}
if (nrow(shared) > 0) {
  n_shared  <- count(shared, cell_type, name = "n_sets")
  le_data   <- shared |>
    left_join(n_shared, by = "cell_type") |>
    mutate(label = paste0(cell_type, "\n(", n_sets, " sets)"))
  deg_point <- deg_overlap |>
    semi_join(le_data, by = "cell_type") |>
    left_join(n_shared, by = "cell_type") |>
    mutate(label = paste0(cell_type, "\n(", n_sets, " sets)"))

  p_F06 <- ggplot(le_data, aes(label, leading_edge_jaccard)) +
    geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = NA, fill = "#e2a9f1", colour = "#8e3fb0", width = 0.6) +
    geom_jitter(aes(colour = collection), width = 0.15, alpha = 0.7, size = 1.6) +
    geom_point(data = deg_point, aes(y = jaccard_DEG, shape = "Overlap of the DEG lists (Step 4)"),
               colour = "black", fill = "#f1a340", size = 4) +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
    scale_shape_manual(values = c("Overlap of the DEG lists (Step 4)" = 23), name = NULL) +
    scale_colour_brewer(palette = "Dark2", name = "Collection") +
    coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
    labs(x = "Cell type (number of shared pathways)",
         y = "Overlap of the driving genes\nin SCZ and BD (Jaccard index)",
         title = "Overlap of the genes driving the pathways shared by SCZ and BD",
         subtitle = "Leading-edge overlap of the pathways altered in the same direction in both disorders (GSEA)",
         caption = "0 = different genes, 1 = same genes. Dashed line: J = 0.5. Diamond: overlap of the DEG lists of the same cell type.") +
    theme_project() +
    guides(colour = guide_legend(order = 1), shape = guide_legend(order = 2))
  print(p_F06)
  save_figure(p_F06, "Q3_F06_leading_edge_overlap", fig_dir, width = 10, height = 6)
} else {
  cat("Note: no shared pathway, the leading-edge comparison cannot be done.\n")
}
```

**Figure Q3-F06 – Overlap of the genes driving the pathways shared by SCZ and BD.** For each gene set significantly
shifted in the same direction in SCZ and BD (GSEA, adjusted p < 0.05 in both), Jaccard index between the leading-edge
genes of the two diseases (dots, coloured by collection; boxes: median and interquartile range per cell type). The
diamond gives, for comparison, the Jaccard index of the DEG lists of the same cell type (Step 4). Dashed line:
J = 0.5.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
Each dot is a pathway changed in the same way in both diseases in one cell type. Low dots: the two diseases reach this
pathway through different genes. High dots: through the same genes. The diamond shows how much the DEG lists overlap.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Interpretation [to fill]"}
- Are most dots below 0.5? Then shared pathways are reached through partly different genes: **H1 is supported**.
- Are the pathways shared even where the DEG overlap (diamond) is low? This is the convergence H1 predicts.
- Close to 1? SCZ and BD share the same genes for these functions: convergence at the gene level too.
- Pick one example pathway with a low overlap and list a few SCZ-only and BD-only driving genes for the report.
:::

# Step 8 – Which results are found by both methods?

**What we do and why.** A pathway found by ORA (with a threshold on genes) **and** by GSEA (without threshold) is more
reliable. For each cell type and disease, we compare the significant sets of the two methods.

```{r ora-gsea-concordance}
ora_all <- bind_rows(
  if (nrow(ora_go_table) > 0) mutate(ora_go_table, collection = "GO_BP"),
  ora_curated_table
)

concordance <- NULL
if (nrow(ora_all) > 0) {
  ora_sig <- ora_all |>
    mutate(disease = sub("_(up|down)$", "", Cluster)) |>
    distinct(collection, cell_type, disease, ID) |>
    mutate(in_ORA = TRUE)
  gsea_sig <- gsea_all |>
    filter(p.adjust < alpha, disease %in% c("SCZ", "BD")) |>
    distinct(collection, cell_type, disease = as.character(disease), ID) |>
    mutate(in_GSEA = TRUE)
  concordance <- full_join(ora_sig, gsea_sig, by = c("collection", "cell_type", "disease", "ID")) |>
    mutate(across(c(in_ORA, in_GSEA), ~ coalesce(.x, FALSE)),
           found_by = case_when(in_ORA & in_GSEA ~ "both", in_ORA ~ "ORA_only", TRUE ~ "GSEA_only"))
  write.csv(concordance, file.path(out_dir, "ora_gsea_concordance.csv"), row.names = FALSE)
  count(concordance, collection, found_by) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = found_by, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)
}
```

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
Number of significant sets found by both methods (`both`), by ORA only or by GSEA only. GO terms of the ORA were
merged with `simplify()`, so the GO overlap is a lower bound.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Interpretation [to fill]"}
- Prefer the pathways found by both methods in the report: they are the most robust.
- Many `GSEA_only` pathways = small coordinated changes that do not pass the DEG threshold: expected under H1.
- `ORA_only` pathways are often driven by a few strongly changed genes.
:::

# Step 9 – Focus on synaptic gene sets (SynGO)

**What we do and why.** The question asks specifically about synaptic and neurotransmission pathways. SynGO is a
database of synaptic genes curated by experts, so it tests this part directly. In the literature, synaptic genes are
mostly down-regulated in excitatory and inhibitory neurons in SCZ [7] (single-nucleus DLPFC); evidence
is scarcer for BD. Glial cells are not expected to show SynGO changes: for them, myelination and inflammation are more
relevant (also followed in Q5). We use SynGO release 1.3: the two top-level terms ("synapse" and "process in the
synapse") and their direct children (for example presynapse, postsynapse, synaptic signalling, synapse organisation);
each term includes the genes of its sub-terms. Terms with fewer than `r min_set_size` tested genes are left out by GSEA.

```{r fig-F07, fig.width=10, fig.height=5}
if ("SynGO" %in% names(collections)) {
  syngo_res <- gsea_all |>
    filter(collection == "SynGO") |>
    mutate(set = clean_set_name(Description, 50))
  lim_s <- max(abs(syngo_res$NES), na.rm = TRUE)

  p_F07 <- ggplot(syngo_res, aes(cell_type, set)) +
    geom_point(aes(size = -log10(p.adjust), colour = NES)) +
    geom_point(data = filter(syngo_res, p.adjust < alpha), aes(size = -log10(p.adjust)),
               shape = 1, colour = "black", stroke = 0.8) +
    facet_wrap(~ disease, labeller = as_labeller(lab_disease)) +
    scale_colour_nes(lim_s) +
    scale_size_continuous(name = "-log10(adjusted p)", range = c(1.5, 8)) +
    labs(x = "Cell type", y = "SynGO term",
         title = "Synaptic gene sets (SynGO) per cell type",
         subtitle = "GSEA on SynGO synaptic gene sets (expert-curated)",
         caption = paste0("Black ring: adjusted p < ", alpha, ". Purple: shifted down; orange: shifted up (right panel: higher in SCZ than in BD).")) +
    theme_project() +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1), legend.position = "right")
  print(p_F07)
  save_figure(p_F07, "Q3_F07_SynGO", fig_dir, width = 10, height = 3 + 0.35 * n_distinct(syngo_res$set))

  paired |>
    filter(collection == "SynGO") |>
    select(cell_type, ID, NES_SCZ, p.adjust_SCZ, NES_BD, p.adjust_BD, group) |>
    arrange(cell_type, pmin(p.adjust_SCZ, p.adjust_BD))
} else {
  cat("Note: SynGO file not available yet, see 01_DATA/genesets/README.md\n")
}
```

**Figure Q3-F07 – Synaptic gene sets (SynGO) per cell type.** GSEA results of the SynGO gene sets, per cell type, in
SCZ vs controls, BD vs controls and SCZ vs BD. Colour: NES (purple = shifted down, orange = shifted up); size:
−log10 adjusted p-value; black ring: adjusted p < 0.05.

::: {.callout-tip title="How to read"}
Each dot is a synaptic gene set in one cell type. Big purple dots with a ring in neurons would mean that synaptic genes
are significantly decreased. The table below gives the values and the category of Figure F03.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Interpretation [to fill]"}
- Are synaptic sets down-regulated (NES < 0) in neurons, in both diseases? Is it significant?
- Stronger in excitatory or in inhibitory neurons?
- Do we reproduce the SCZ result of Ruzicka et al. [7]? What do we add for BD?
:::

**Links with the other questions.**

- **Q2**: shared genes vs shared functions: is the convergence stronger at the pathway level?
- **Q4**: shared pathways involving ligands, receptors or neurotransmission can be checked in the CellChat results.
- **Q5**: inflammation and myelination pathways found here are also followed as ageing signatures.

# Limits to discuss in the report

- **Dependence on Q2.** The enrichment inherits every bias of the DE analysis (covariates, number of donors per cell
  type).
- **Threshold of the ORA.** ORA results depend on the DEG cut-off; GSEA does not, which is why both are reported.
- **Redundancy of GO.** Even after merging, report a few representative terms, not long lists of synonyms.
- **Annotation bias.** Well-studied genes belong to more gene sets and weigh more in the results.
- **RNA is not activity.** A pathway shifted at the RNA level does not prove a change in protein activity.
- **Medication.** Antipsychotics (SCZ) and lithium or mood stabilisers (BD) can change synaptic and metabolic genes on
  their own. A pathway that differs between SCZ and BD may reflect the treatment rather than the disease.
- **Power.** A disease with fewer donors has fewer significant pathways: "specific" may mean "not detected". The direct
  SCZ vs BD test limits this risk, but it has less power than the comparisons with controls, and a non-significant
  direct test does not prove that the two diseases are identical.

# List of figures

All figures are saved as `.png` in `04_FIGURES/Q3/`. We kept only the figures
that answer a part of the question; intermediate results (numbers of DEGs, numbers of shifted pathways, ORA vs GSEA
agreement...) are tables, because they are checks rather than results. The proposed placement follows the logic of a
scientific article: **main** figures answer the question and test the hypothesis (slides and report);
**supplementary** figures support them (appendix). To be confirmed with the real results.

| Figure | File | What it shows | Why we need it | Proposed placement |
|--------|------|---------------|----------------|--------------------|
| F01 | `Q3_F01_ORA_GO_<cell type>` | GO terms over-represented among the DEGs, per key cell type | first answer to "which functions?", close to the Q2 genes (ORA step of the workflow) | Supplementary; one cell type in the report if the result is clear |
| F02 | `Q3_F02_GSEA_example` | one GSEA result in detail | lets the reader (and the jury) understand NES and leading edge, used in all the next figures | Supplementary (or methods slide) |
| F03 | `Q3_F03_pathway_categories` | shared vs specific pathways per cell type, specific ones checked by the direct SCZ vs BD test | answers "shared or specific?" with the right test | **Main** |
| F04 | `Q3_F04_NES_scatter_Hallmark` | NES in SCZ against NES in BD for every process | shows whether the two profiles are similar overall, beyond significant pathways | Supplementary (main if the correlation is a key result) |
| F05 | `Q3_F05_NES_heatmap_Hallmark` / `_GO_BP` | the main pathways in SCZ, BD and SCZ vs BD | names the pathways that are shared and those that differ | **Main** (Hallmark); GO version supplementary |
| F06 | `Q3_F06_leading_edge_overlap` | overlap of the genes driving the shared pathways, compared with the DEG overlap | **direct test of H1**: same function, different genes? | **Main** |
| F07 | `Q3_F07_SynGO` | synaptic gene sets per cell type | answers the synaptic part of the question | **Main** (report); slide if the result is clear |

For the slides (1–2 per question): F05 (which pathways) and F06 (H1). For the report: F03, F05, F06 and F07 in the
main text; F01, F02, F04 and F05-GO in the appendix.
